title: Three more attributes we see in learning-focused leaders and managers
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton continues his list of attributes of learning-focused school leaders with three more. First, they are servant leaders who see their job as enabling classroom teachers, the people who actually produce learning, and who accept accountability for doing so. Second, they build structures and systems that serve learning, illustrated by an international school that counted more than 400 activities, found about half unrelated to learning, and paused them to relieve overload. Third, they put coaching at the centre of professional development, grounded in evidence gathered by walking classrooms, rather than relying on distant courses of uncertain impact. He treats teaching as a skill best improved in real time, drawing on Education Week's critique of the teacher PD market.
points: Servant leadership in a school means leaders exist to enable teachers' classroom work, with mutual accountability, and is not a soft option.
Leaders should ask what each system adds to student learning and cut those that merely control teachers or consume their energy.
One school's audit found only about half of 400 simultaneous activities contributed to learning, which led its director to pause the rest.
Coaching teachers in their own classrooms, designed from leaders' evidence, develops the skill of teaching better than off-site courses.
quotes: Servant leadership places the role of leaders as servants to others rather than being served by others. Servant leadership puts leaders and managers in the same relationship to their colleagues and students as those teachers who have changed from being the stars of their classrooms to the roadies. Putting learning at the very centre of the school makes leaders and managers the roadies to their teaching colleagues.

Leaders and managers in learning-focused schools become servant leaders because they recognise that the fundamental work of the school - student learning - happens in classrooms and is facilitated and enabled by teachers. They know that it is not happening in their offices.
Servant leadership might sound soft to some testosterone fuelled leaders of schools. It is anything but.
Systems, structures and processes are important to any organisation. They are the scaffolding that holds everything together. But they are not good by default.

Their conclusions surprised them. They counted more than 400 individual activities taking place at any one moment across this big school and identified just over 200 of them as making an identifiable contribution towards student learning.

Most of the teacher ‘development’ that then takes place later during a teacher’s career, is off-site, not classroom-based and, in many cases, voluntary. It is possible in some countries and some schools for teachers to spend 40 years in the profession and have only minimal further classroom-focused professional development once they have left college.

They know, as research is now beginning to validate, that teaching for learning is essentially a skill. It is something that teachers are able to do, to greater or lesser degrees. They know that teacher knowledge content is important but not as important as the skills involved in creating effective learning in classrooms, lesson after lesson, day after day.
